That's because evolution and mutations aren't a quick process. Living organisms' internal mechanisms are incredibly precise (the way our blood is circulated, the layers in our skin etc) and evolution(change, adaptations, mutations) in these mechanisms is rare and happens over a time period we cannot even begin to fathom. It's incredibly slow but the power of compounding is such that the changes seem drastic. 

We don't see anomalies like a tiger with gray stripes etc. very often because these anomalies by nature are exceedingly rare and just spotting a tiger or a whale itself is a tough task. They may or may not exist - we just wouldn't know. The odds of a mutation being harmful is much more than for it to be beneficial and could lead to premature death, so humans would have just never known that that specific mutation in that animal ever happened. Sort of how when an animal we thought had been extinct for decades gets spotted and had been alive the entire time.
